Q1.answer: (a) The main 2026 rule is OPM's 'Reduction in Force' final rule, FR Doc. 2026-15665, 91 FR 49178 (pp. 49178-49227), published August 3, 2026, effective September 2, 2026. Docket OPM-2025-0107; RIN 3206-AO86. (b) The proposed rule it finalized is FR Doc. 2026-04377, 91 FR 10904, published March 5, 2026 (same docket and RIN). (c) Corrections to the final rule through November 14, 2026: (1) FR Doc. 2026-17335, 91 FR 54794, published August 25, 2026, effective September 2, 2026. It fixes typographical and clerical errors: amendatory instructions 15, 36 and 39 (instruction 36 targeted 351.802(a) text that does not exist), 'of this part' references to 11.2 and 11.3 changed to 'of this title', defective list structure in 330.202 and 351.702(a)(4)(iv), part 316 typos, and it conforms the part 351 authority citation to the appeals rule. (2) FR Doc. 2026-18800, 91 FR 58363, published September 15, 2026, effective September 15, 2026. Instruction 11 inadvertently removed paragraphs (1)(i) and (1)(ii) of the 'displaced' definition in 330.602; the correction restores them. (d) The rule's Dates paragraph says an agency that issued a RIF notice before September 2, 2026 must process the RIF under the regulations in effect when the notice was issued, and an agency that issues a notice on or after that date must apply the amended provisions. The same split is restated in the Implementation Considerations discussion (91 FR 49206-07). Reductions in force with notices issued before September 2 stay under the earlier rules. (e) Other 2026 final rules that amend 5 CFR part 351 (not corrections): (i) FR Doc. 2026-15666, 'Reduction in Force Appeals', 91 FR 49230, effective September 2, 2026. It rewrites subpart I (351.901-351.909) and 351.802(a)(6), applies only to RIF notices issued on or after September 2, and is in force today. (ii) FR Doc. 2026-21316, 'Managing Senior Professional Performance', 91 FR 65904, effective November 18, 2026. It makes conforming changes in part 351 (authority citation, the 351.203 'rating of record' definition, and 351.503 cross-references). It is not yet in force. (iii) FR Doc. 2026-21320, 'Administrative Leave for Workforce Realignment and Other Purposes', 91 FR 65924, effective November 18, 2026. It revises 351.806 (status during notice period). It is not yet in force. Excluded: FR Doc. 2026-13715, 91 FR 41521, effective August 6, 2026, also lists part 351, but its effective date is before September 2.
Q1.basis: fr_doc 2026-15665 (citation, dates, docket, RIN, CFR list). fr_doc 2026-04377 (proposed rule). 2026-17335 pp. 54794-54795 (summary and list of errors). 2026-18800 pp. 58363-58364 (Background, Need for Correction, amendatory instruction 2). 2026-15665 Dates paragraph (p. 49178) and Implementation Considerations (pp. 49206-49207). 2026-15666 DATES (p. 49230). CFR-part search (cfr 5:351, since 2026-01-01) and fr_doc on 2026-21320, 2026-21316, 2026-13715 for CFR-affected lists. 2026-21320 amendatory text, 91 FR 65939 (new 351.806) and 65940 (630.1403(c)(10)).
Q1.uncertainty: The CFR is not available, so I could not confirm the codified text of part 351 after each amendment. The 2026-21316 part 351 changes were checked only by grep and the preamble, not by reading the whole amendatory text. The search returned 2026-15654 (probationary appeals) and 2026-15650 (suitability) but neither is indexed as amending part 351; I did not read them. The appeals correction (2026-17338, 91 FR 54796) corrects 2026-15666, not the main rule, so it is not counted in (c).

Q2.answer: (a) Performance credit, veterans' points, total (notices issued September 3, 2026; three most recent ratings within the 4 years before issuance; values 7/5/3/0 for Levels 5/4/3/2). Abbott: 7+5+5=17; not a preference eligible, so 0 points; total 17; subgroup B; tenure subgroup I (career). Bianchi: 5+0+3=8; preference eligible with a 30% compensable disability, so +5 (subgroup AD); total 13; subgroup I. Castillo: 7+5+5=17; retired Army lieutenant colonel with 22 years and retired pay based on length of service. Under 351.504(b)(2) this fails (retired pay is based on 20 or more years), and (b)(4) requires a disabled veteran, which he is not. So not a preference eligible, 0 points, total 17, subgroup B, tenure subgroup I. Dalton: only two ratings, Level 5 (7) and Level 2 (0). Proxy = (7+0)/2 = 3.5, so performance credit = 3.5+7+0 = 10.5; preference eligible with no disability, so +3 (subgroup A); total 13.5; tenure subgroup I. Eze: term appointment of four years is not a career or career-conditional appointment and is not a temporary appointment of one year or less, so tenure subgroup II under 351.502(a)(3). Performance 5+5+5=15; no preference; total 15. Fontaine: one rating, Level 4, so 5x3=15 under 351.503(f)(3); no preference; total 15; tenure subgroup I. (b) Ranking within the competitive service tenure group by total, then tenure subgroup, then earliest SCD (351.501(b)-(c)): 1. Abbott 17 (I, SCD 5/1/2003); 2. Castillo 17 (I, SCD 8/1/2012); 3. Fontaine 15 (I, SCD 6/15/2015); 4. Eze 15 (II, SCD 2/5/2009); 5. Dalton 13.5 (A, II? no: subgroup I, SCD 3/19/2018); 6. Bianchi 13 (AD, I, SCD 9/10/2007). Ties: Abbott and Castillo tie at 17; both are subgroup I, so the earlier SCD (Abbott, 2003) ranks higher. Fontaine and Eze tie at 15; Fontaine is subgroup I and Eze subgroup II, so Fontaine ranks higher. Released: Bianchi (13) and Dalton (13.5), the two lowest. Note: Dalton is subgroup I (career), not II. (c) Under the earlier rules as the 2026 preamble describes them, Bianchi would rank above Abbott. Employees are ranked first by tenure group, then by veterans' subgroup AD, A, B, and only then by length of service adjusted by performance (91 FR 49198). Bianchi (AD) therefore outranks Abbott (B) before any performance comparison. (d) Under 351.506(c)(1) she may inspect the complete retention register for her level, including the names of all other employees on it and the retention information used (performance credit as augmented by veterans' preference, and SCD), so that she can see how the level was constructed and how standing was determined. Under 351.506(c)(2) and (e) she may also see other registers that affect her assignment rights, subject to FOIA and the Privacy Act.
Q2.uncertainty: The text on the order of release in 351.601(a)-(b) is not reprinted here; I assumed release proceeds from the lowest standing. Eze's appointment is assumed to be a competitive-service term appointment, as the scenario says. The earlier rules are described only through the 2026 preamble, not their codified text. Under 351.506(c)(1) the text says 'the names of all other employees listed on that register' and 'relevant retention information', but does not expressly say whether individual ratings of others must be shown, so the scope of disclosure is not fully settled.

Q3.answer: (a) A: Not a preference eligible. 0 points. Subgroup B. Deciding paragraph: 351.504(b). Retired pay is based on 22 years, so (b)(2) fails. There is no disability retirement or armed-conflict basis, so (b)(1) fails. (b)(3) does not apply. (b)(4) only applies to a disabled veteran who meets (b)(1)-(3), and he has no disability. B: Not a preference eligible. 0 points. Subgroup B. Retired pay is based on 21 years of service, so (b)(2) fails; the retirement is not disability-based, so (b)(1) fails; (b)(4) cannot make him eligible on its own. C: Preference eligible. 5 points. Subgroup AD. Deciding paragraphs: 351.504(b)(1)(i) (disability retirement for injury in line of duty as a direct result of armed conflict), (b)(4) (retired at major, and a disabled veteran), and (a)(1) (compensable disability of 60%, at least 30%). D: Not a preference eligible. 0 points. Subgroup B. Retired pay based on 24 years fails (b)(2); no disability basis; (b)(4) applies only to major or above, and he is a master sergeant. E: Preference eligible. 3 points. Subgroup A. Deciding paragraphs: 351.504(b)(2), since retired pay is based on 16 years, which is less than 20; and (a)(2) (disability of 10%, under 30%). (b)(1) does not apply because the injury was not from armed conflict or an instrumentality of war. (b) SCD computation under 351.505(d): SCD = appointment date minus total prior creditable service. A is not a preference eligible, so only active service in a war or in a campaign with a badge is creditable (351.505(b)(2)(i)). Credit = 2 years. SCD = September 7, 2010 minus 2 years = September 7, 2008. C is a preference eligible, so all active service is creditable under 351.505(b)(2)(ii). Credit = 14 years. SCD = September 7, 2010 minus 14 years = September 7, 1996. (c) The subgroups mark which points were added (AD = 5, A = 3, B = 0) under 351.504(a) and must be shown on the register and in the notice (351.802(a)(2)). Points are added to performance credit before ranking (351.501(b)). The subgroup itself is not a separate sort key in 351.501(c); ties are broken by tenure subgroup and then by SCD. Because the points are already part of the total, two employees with the same total are tied regardless of subgroup.
Q3.uncertainty: Each deciding paragraph is applied as printed. The text of 5 U.S.C. 2108(2) (the definition of disabled veteran) is not reprinted, so I did not test the disabled-veteran element for C beyond the scenario's 60% rating. Length-of-service credit for C depends on the scenario's statement that all 14 years are active service.

Q4.answer: (a) Farah's three most recent ratings received within the 4 years before September 3, 2026 (window opens September 3, 2022): August 10, 2026 Level 5 = 7; November 14, 2025 Level 3 = 3; November 15, 2024 Level 3 = 3. Performance credit = 7+3+3 = 13. The November 2022 and November 2023 ratings are older than the three most recent. (b) Cutoff date = 45 days before September 3, 2026 = July 20, 2026 (July 20 to July 31 is 11 days, August is 31 days, September 1-3 is 3 days; 11+31+3 = 45). Ratings put on record after July 20 cannot be used. Farah's August 10 rating is excluded. Her three most recent ratings within 4 years before the cutoff (window opens July 20, 2022): November 14, 2025 = 3; November 15, 2024 = 3; November 20, 2023 = 5. Performance credit = 11. (c) No. Under 351.503(c)(2) a cutoff means no new ratings of record will be put on record and used after the cutoff date. Under 351.503(c)(3) a rating counts only if it has been issued with all reviews and signatures and is on record, meaning available to the office that builds registers. This rating was not on record until August 15, 2026, after the July 20 cutoff, so it cannot be used even though it was given to the employee on July 15. (d) Gina: the August 15, 2022 rating falls outside the window opening September 3, 2022, so only two ratings count. Under 351.503(f)(2) the proxy is the average of the two actual values: (5+3)/2 = 4. Performance credit = 4 + 5 + 3 = 12. (e) Hank has no rating of record in the period. Under 351.503(f)(1) his credit is based on the modal rating for the summary-level pattern that applies to his position of record at the time of the RIF. The other agency's ratings are not ratings of record unless the agency has determined they are equivalent under 351.503(b)(3). The FR text does not state the modal value or the arithmetic for a no-rating employee, so I cannot give a number.
Q4.basis: 2026-15665: 351.503(c)(1)-(4) (pp. 49220-49222); 351.503(f)(1)-(3) (p. 49222); 351.503(b)(1),(3) (p. 49221); 351.203 'rating of record' (p. 49219) and the 'modal rating' reference in 351.503(f)(1), which is not reprinted. Dates computation: 45-day count shown above. Preamble on modal ratings: 91 FR 49193 and 49203.
Q4.uncertainty: The text of 'modal rating' in 351.203 is not reprinted in the 2026 rule, so Hank's credit cannot be computed from the FR text. Q4(c) assumes that the agency's conditions for 'received' do not override the on-record requirement in 351.503(c)(3). Q4(b)-(d) assume the notices were issued on September 3, 2026, as the question's opening sentence states.

Q5.answer: (a) (i) Notices August 28, 2026 (before September 2): the earlier rules apply (Dates paragraph). Under the earlier rules as the 2026 preamble describes them, ranking is by tenure group, then veterans' subgroup (both B), then adjusted SCD. Performance is converted to years of service: three Level 3 ratings average to 12 years, and three Level 5 ratings average to 20 years (91 FR 49186). Lee: 1998-03-02 minus 12 years = 1986-03-02. Park: 2019-07-08 minus 20 years = 1999-07-08. The earlier adjusted SCD ranks first, so Lee is retained and Park is released. (ii) Notices September 2, 2026: the amended rules apply. Lee: 3+3+3 = 9. Park: 7+7+7 = 21. Park ranks higher, so Lee is released. (iii) Notices September 3, 2026: same new-rules result, so Lee is released. The October 27 or November 2 effective dates do not change which rules apply. (b) No. A notice that only changes the effective date is not a new specific RIF notice, and the agency need not redetermine or recalculate retention standing (351.805(b), p. 49226). Standing is fixed as of receipt of the specific notice (351.507(a)), and the four-year window runs back from the issuance date of the notices (351.503(c)(1)). Lee's October 15 Level 5 rating is outside that window and after the notice date, so it cannot count. The only permitted correction is of an agency error (351.507(c)). (c) (1) Which version applies: the date the agency issues the specific RIF notice (Dates paragraph of 2026-15665, p. 49178; Implementation, p. 49207). (2) The end of the four-year period for ratings: the date the RIF notices are issued, or the agency-established cutoff date if one is used (351.503(c)(1)-(2), p. 49220). (3) Tenure subgroup and retention standing: the date the employee receives a specific RIF notice (351.502(a)(2)-(3), p. 49220; 351.507(a), p. 49223).
Q5.uncertainty: The codified earlier rules are not in the FR text. I relied on the preamble's description of the earlier method (91 FR 49186, 49198) for the adjusted-SCD arithmetic. I assumed both employees' listed ratings were within the four-year window and were rated under one pattern. Q5(b) assumes the October 20 amended notice changed only the effective date.

Q6.answer: (a) Jordan qualifies for assignment rights, because he has a current annual rating of Level 2, which is at the threshold in 351.701(a). The rule requires an offer to the position that requires no reduction, or the least possible reduction, in representative rate, from among qualifying positions. Each candidate: (1) GS-12 Ellis: lower standing, same area, full time, one grade below. Available. (2) GS-11 Frank: lower standing, two grades below. Available, but a larger reduction than Ellis. (3) GS-10 Gale: lower standing, three grades below (the limit for a non-30% preference eligible). Available, but a larger reduction. (4) GS-9 Hana: four grades below. Not available, because the limit is three grades (351.701(b)(2)). (5) GS-12 Ito: higher standing. Not available (351.701(b)(1)). (6) GS-12 part-time Kim: different work schedule. Not available (351.701(a)). (7) GS-12 Lund: different competitive area. Not available (351.701(a)). The agency must offer GS-12 Ellis. (b) A preference eligible with a 30% compensable disability has a five-grade limit (351.701(b)(2)), so GS-9 Hana becomes within reach. But the rule still requires the least reduction in rate, so the agency must still offer GS-12 Ellis. (c) A Level 1 rating is below the Level 2 threshold in 351.701(a). Jordan has no assignment right, and none of the seven positions has to be offered under Part 351. (d) Assignment rights under 351.701 apply only to competitive service tenure group employees. For excepted service employees, 351.705(a) lets an agency adopt assignment rights 'on the same basis' as 351.701 at its discretion. So nothing is required by the rule. (e) The 2026 documents do not support the old handbook. Former 351.701(d), which barred a Level 2 employee from taking a position held by a higher-rated employee, was eliminated (91 FR 49204). 'Bump and retreat' is replaced by a single assignment right to a position held by a lower-standing employee in the same tenure group (91 FR 49178, item 12; 49198). So there is no separate bumping or retreating step.
Q6.uncertainty: The printed 351.701(a) requires that the position be in the same competitive area. For Ito and Lund the scenario says 'higher standing' and 'different competitive area', which I applied as stated. The rule does not say how the agency orders multiple offers when several qualifying positions exist; here the least-reduction rule settles it.

Q7.answer: (a) The MSPB hears the appeal. The notice was issued August 31, before the September 2, 2026 effective date. The Dates paragraph of 2026-15665 says the earlier regulations govern, and the appeals rule's DATES says it applies only to specific RIF notices issued on or after September 2. The MSPB's 2026 rule removes RIF appeals from 1201.3 but keeps adjudicating RIF appeals where the notice was issued before that date. The MSPB's text (91 FR 51997-51998) does not say which timeline applies. (b) OPM hears the appeal (351.901(a)). The notice was issued October 19, after the effective date. Morgan must file electronically through OPM's e-filing system identified on OPM's website (351.902(a)). OPM will not accept email or postal filings absent good cause and prior OPM approval. Deadline: 351.902(b) gives 30 calendar days from the effective date of the action, December 18, 2026. The first day counted is December 19. Day 30 is January 17, 2027, which is a Sunday. Under 351.902(b)(1) the period runs to the first workday after that, but Monday January 18, 2027 is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, a federal holiday, so the last day is Tuesday January 19, 2027, 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. (c) Morgan must prove by a preponderance of the evidence (351.901(b)): (1) timeliness; (2) that OPM has jurisdiction; (3) that the agency failed to comply with an applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions; and (4) that the failure prejudiced her by causing the action or the loss of a materially more favorable outcome. She is not entitled to a hearing as of right. Under 351.905(c) OPM decides on the written record, and holds a hearing only if it finds one necessary and efficient. (d) Under 351.901(c)(2) a RIF action taken under part 351 and any matter relating to its appeal 'may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration'. The preamble says the rule does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs. When agreements are renegotiated, the rule limits agencies' duty and ability to bargain for provisions creating a direct RIF appeal process. Questions about the effect of particular existing provisions remain for the chapter 71 forum (91 FR 49245). (e) No. Under 351.901(c)(4) a party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under subpart I, and under 351.909(e) there is no further right of appeal of OPM's final decision. (f) Yes, but only within the collateral-matter tolling rule. Morgan timely filed an OSC complaint before the appeal deadline, and under 351.902(b)(3) she may file a RIF appeal within 30 calendar days after the OSC decision becomes final and no longer subject to further administrative review, if the decision materially affects her retention standing. If March 10, 2027 is the date it became final and no further review applies, the 30 days run from March 10: March 11 is day 1 and April 9, 2027 is day 30, a Friday. So the last day would be April 9, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. OPM decides in its sole discretion whether the decision materially affects her rights. (g) The decisive text is the Dates paragraph of the appeals rule (91 FR 49230): 'This final rule applies only to a RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026'. It is matched by the Dates paragraph of 2026-15665 (91 FR 49178): an agency that issued a notice before the effective date processes under the earlier regulations. Preamble at 91 FR 49236 and 49262 repeats the point.
Q7.uncertainty: The MSPB's own filing deadlines and procedures are not reprinted here, so I could not state Morgan's MSPB deadline in (a). For (f), the answer depends on the date the OSC decision becomes final and no longer subject to review; if further review follows, the period moves. OPM also decides whether the rating correction 'materially affects' her retention standing. The union's CBA is not in the record, so I cannot say whether its grievance clause covers this action.

Q8.answer: (a) Today (November 14, 2026) the 351.806 in force is the pre-change text. The FR documents describe it as directing that an employee be kept in duty status 'when possible', and as addressing emergency leave without pay in its paragraph on emergencies (91 FR 39034; 91 FR 49-note in 2026-21320 at 65926 and 65936). The full text of that version is not reprinted in the documents I read. The adopted text is in the final rule 2026-21320 (91 FR 65924; new 351.806 at 91 FR 65939), effective November 18, 2026. It is not in force today. Its paragraphs: (a) under ordinary circumstances an employee remains in duty status during the notice period; (b) the agency may place the employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period when it determines such leave is appropriate, consistent with 5 CFR part 630, subpart N; (c) in an emergency lack of work or funds, the agency may place the employee on annual leave with or without consent, on leave without pay with consent, or in nonpay status without consent. (b) Under the adopted 351.806(b) no consent is required. The companion provision, new 630.1403(c)(10) (91 FR 65940), allows administrative leave for an employee subject to RIF separation between receipt of the notice and separation when the agency determines it is in the Government's best interests. It has no stated day limit. Subsections (c)(9) and (c)(11) are expressly subject to Governmentwide limits (currently 12 weeks absent OPM and OMB approval of a higher threshold), and the preamble says the rule does not authorize unlimited leave and retains the principle that leave be limited to the amount reasonably necessary (91 FR 65927). An agency may still set its own limits. (c) Before the adopted text takes effect, the preamble says the current 351.806 directs keeping RIF employees in duty status 'when possible', and OPM's Agency Policy Template said an agency may provide administrative leave during a RIF notice period if it determines such use supports agency interests (91 FR 39034, in the proposed rule). (d) No. The final rule says it does not waive, suspend or displace any part 351 requirement, and that retention registers, retention standing, veterans' preference and all other RIF requirements continue to apply in full to any involuntary RIF separation (91 FR 65926). Retention standing is fixed as of receipt of the specific notice (351.507(a)). Notice and appeal rights in subparts H and I are not changed by the leave rule.
Q8.uncertainty: The pre-change 351.806 text is not reproduced in any FR document I read, so (a) relies on the 2026 preambles' descriptions. The leave taken on October 26 was under the pre-change text, since the adopted text takes effect November 18. No Governmentwide duration limit applies to (c)(10) by its terms; whether the 12-week cap applies to it by implication is not stated in the text. The adopted rule does not state a consent requirement for (b) in either direction, so the answer rests on the absence of such language.

Q9.answer: Step 1 does not comply. The Tulsa field office was designated as a competitive area on August 17, 2026, which is 57 days before the October 13 notices. Under 351.402(c) an area established within 90 days before notices must be submitted to OPM for approval in advance, with a bona fide organizational basis statement. Nothing was sent to OPM, so the requirement is not met. Designation is also limited to the head of the agency or a designee at headquarters level or above (351.402(b)(1)); the designee's level is not stated. Step 2 complies. Novak is a career-conditional employee serving an initial probationary period, so she is excluded from RIF competition under 351.202(d)(2)(ii), and the agency may retain her while releasing a competing employee under 351.202(d)(3). Step 3 does not comply. A supervisory probationary period is not an initial probationary period (351.203 'Initial probationary period' excludes the period applicable on initial appointment to a supervisory position). Ortiz has career tenure and is not serving an initial probationary period, so she is tenure subgroup I (351.502(a)(2)). She must be ranked on the register like any competing employee. Step 4 does not comply. The cutoff is 30 days before October 13, i.e., September 13. A rating put on record October 2 is after the cutoff and cannot be used under 351.503(c)(2). The cutoff must be applied uniformly within the competitive area (351.503(c)(4)), so Pruitt's rating must be disregarded. Step 5 does not comply. Quist has two actual ratings, so 351.503(f)(2) requires the proxy to be the average of the two actual values: (7+5)/2 = 6. Her performance credit is 6+7+5 = 18, not 15. A presumed Level 3 is not the rule. Step 6 does not comply. Section 351.503(d) allows additional points only where the highest summary level is a Level 3 (pass/fail or the former pattern D). This agency uses a five-level pattern, and the additional points are limited to Level 3 employees with documented exceptional performance. A written policy announced in advance does not extend the rule to everyone. Step 7 complies. Under 351.601(c), if competing employees have identical performance credit, the same tenure subgroup and identical SCD, the agency may select any tied employee for release. Step 8 does not comply. Under 351.602(a) an agency may not release a competing employee while retaining in that level an employee with a specifically limited temporary or term promotion. Reyes must not be retained while another employee in the level is released. Step 9 complies. Under 351.702(a)(4)(v) no assessment is required if, during the five years ending on the date of the notice, the employee occupied the same position and received a Level 3 or higher rating for it. Silva held the position until 2023 (within the window ending October 13, 2026) and received a Level 4 rating in 2022. Step 10 does not comply. Under 351.702(a)(4)(iii) an assessment may not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment. The questionnaire must be replaced by an assessment that meets 351.702(a)(4)(i)-(iii). Step 11 does not comply. Under 351.608(a)(3) exceptions may not be sequenced or stacked. A single exception is limited: 90 days under (b) for undue interruption and up to 90 days under (g). Sixty days plus sixty days is 120 days and stacks two exceptions. The agency must choose one exception, not exceeding 90 days, and must give the notices required by 351.608(a)(4) for periods over 30 days. Step 12 does not comply. The notice must state the right to appeal to OPM, the time limit under 351.902(b), and the electronic filing system on OPM's website (351.802(a)(6)). An appeal to MSPB is no longer available for a notice issued on or after September 2 (351.901(a); 2026-16456 removes RIF appeals from 1201.3 except Foreign Service). The 30-day period runs from the effective date, which is correct.
Q9.uncertainty: Step 1: whether the designee's level is at headquarters is not stated, so I could not decide that part. Step 7: the rule permits selection among exactly tied employees, but the write-up does not say whether the two employees were in the same competitive level. Step 11: 'undue interruption' might be argued under 351.607, but that section applies before the effective date, not after. The codified text of the earlier 351.806 is not reprinted (see Q8).

Q10.answer: (a) On September 10, 2026 paragraph (1) of the 'displaced' definition in 330.602 contained only its introductory text, as revised by amendatory instruction 11 of the final rule. Paragraphs (1)(i) and (1)(ii) were not in the text. Instruction 11 directed revision of paragraph (1) but set out only the introductory text, which had the effect of removing (1)(i) and (1)(ii) (91 FR 49217). OPM intended to revise only the introductory text. (b) The change to the 'displaced' definition was made by the final rule 2026-15665, published August 3, 2026, effective September 2, 2026. It replaced references to career and career-conditional (tenure group I or II) employees with the competitive service tenure group. The accidental deletion of (1)(i) and (1)(ii) was corrected by FR Doc. 2026-18800, published September 15, 2026, effective September 15, 2026. OPM acted without notice and comment under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). The correction 'makes no substantive change', restores text that was in effect before September 2 that OPM did not propose to remove and did not discuss removing, and so notice and comment were unnecessary. OPM also found good cause under 553(d)(3) for immediate effect. (c) Under the restored text, paragraph (1)(i) makes a competitive service employee displaced if the employee received a RIF separation notice under part 351 and has not declined an offer under part 351 subpart G of a position with the same type of work schedule and a representative rate at least as high as that of the position from which separated. Nadia received a separation notice, so she is displaced under (1)(i) unless she declined a qualifying offer. (i) Lower representative rate offer, declined: the offer does not meet the 'at least as high' test, so declining it does not end displacement. She is still displaced under (1)(i). (ii) Same representative rate offer, declined: the offer meets the test, so declining it means she is not displaced under (1)(i). Under the text as published on September 2 without (1)(i), she would not meet paragraph (1) at all until the September 15 correction restored it.
Q10.basis: 2026-18800 (91 FR 58363-58364): Background, Need for Correction, Administrative Procedure Act section, and amendatory instruction 2 with the restored text. 2026-15665, amendatory instruction 11 and 330.602 'displaced' and 'surplus' (p. 49217). 351.701(a) (p. 49225) for offers. The CTAP definition is in 330.602 as amended.
Q10.uncertainty: The question's date (September 10) falls between September 2 (rule effective) and September 15 (correction effective). On September 10 the printed text lacked (1)(i) and (ii). Whether the agency must treat the restored text as retroactive to September 2 is not stated in the correction, which says it is effective upon publication and restores text 'in effect before September 2'. For the same reason, whether the September 8 notice falls under the restored text is not expressly resolved. Nadia's notice was received September 8, before the correction.

Q11.answer: Differences found between the proposed regulatory text (2026-04377) and the final regulatory text (2026-15665), limited to the paragraphs I compared: (1) 351.202(d)(1)(ii): proposed 'An employee serving a trial period as of the date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice'; final 'An employee serving a trial period' (the as-of-notice qualifier is dropped). (2) 351.202(d)(2)(iii): proposed 'An employee serving on a temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less under subpart C or D of part 316'; final 'An employee serving under a temporary appointment of one (1) year or less under subpart D of part 316' (the term appointment and subpart C references are dropped). (3) 351.202(d)(3)-(4): proposed (d)(3) says such employees 'may be retained, furloughed, separated, demoted or reassigned without regard to the provisions of this part'; final (d)(3) requires the action to be consistent with the appointment and applicable law, and a new (d)(4) requires a written notice under 351.801 that states the employee was not ranked. (4) 351.504(a)(1)-(3): proposed 'should be identified as being in veterans' preference Subgroup AD/A/B'; final 'must be identified'. (5) 351.701(a): proposed 'minimally successful (Level 2)'; final 'minimally satisfactory (Level 2)'. (6) 351.702(a)(4)(iii): proposed 'Does not solely include or principally rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination'; final 'Does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment'. (7) 351.702(a)(4)(iv): proposed used subparagraphs (A) and (B) for the technical-skill test; final uses a single sentence with (1) and (2). (8) 351.507(b): proposed 'retained under any of this paragraph (b)'; final 'retained under any of these provisions', which now points to 351.606(b), 351.607 and 351.608.
Q11.uncertainty: Not exhaustive. I did not complete a line-by-line comparison of every amended section, including 351.203 definitions, 351.503, 351.505, 351.606, 351.608(a)-(g), 351.802, 351.805 and 330.602. I did not check the final rule's summary of changes against each item. The proposed 351.805(b) text was not located, so I could not compare it. Items (6) and (7) may be wording or format changes rather than substantive changes.

Q12.answer: (a) Register for the GS-13 level. Window: notices issued October 5, 2026, so ratings received October 5, 2022 through October 5, 2026 count. Values: Level 5 = 7, Level 4 = 5, Level 3 = 3, Level 2 = 0. Alvarez: 7+7+5 = 19; no preference; total 19; tenure subgroup I (career); SCD April 4, 2011. Chen: September 30, 2022 rating is outside the window, leaving two ratings: 7 (Nov 14, 2024) and 5 (Nov 13, 2025). Proxy = (7+5)/2 = 6; performance credit = 6+7+5 = 18; no preference; total 18; subgroup I; SCD May 22, 2017. Dube: career-conditional who completed probation; subgroup II under 351.502(a)(3); two ratings, 5 and 5; proxy = 5; performance credit = 5+5+5 = 15; preference eligible with no disability, so +3; total 18; subgroup II; SCD August 3, 2015. Estrada: Level 5 rating received October 20, 2026 is after the notices and cannot be used. Three most recent within window: 5 (Nov 13, 2025), 3 (Nov 14, 2024), 5 (Nov 15, 2023) = 13; preference eligible with no disability, +3; total 16; subgroup I; SCD February 6, 2012. Brandt: 3+5+0 = 8; preference eligible with a 30% disability, +5 (subgroup AD); total 13; subgroup I; SCD January 9, 2014. Farouk: one rating (Level 3 on November 14, 2024); performance credit = 3x3 = 9; no preference; total 9; subgroup I; SCD October 1, 2019. He is restoration protected: 14 months of uniformed service is more than 180 days, so retention protection runs one year after restoration (through July 13, 2027) under 353.209(b) as described in the preamble (91 FR 49203). Quinn is not on the register because she is a career-conditional employee serving an initial probationary period, excluded under 351.202(d)(2)(ii). Order of retention (highest to lowest): Alvarez 19; Chen 18 (I); Dube 18 (II); Estrada 16; Brandt 13; Farouk 9. (b) Released: Brandt (13), Estrada (16) and Dube (18, subgroup II). Farouk, the lowest, is restoration protected, so under 351.606(a)(2) he may not be released while another competing employee may be released instead; the agency passes him over and releases the next lowest. Dube and Chen tie at 18, and 351.501(c) breaks the tie by tenure subgroup, so Dube (II) is lower and is released. Chen and Alvarez are retained. (c) Offers under 351.701(b): Brandt (5-grade limit; lower standing only Ikeda at 9): must be offered Ikeda's GS-9 position, four grades below, the only lower-standing position within his limit. Estrada (3-grade limit; lower-standing positions Hill 14 at GS-11 and Jones 15 at GS-10; Gomez 17 is higher): must be offered Hill's GS-11 position, the least reduction in rate. Dube (3-grade limit; lower-standing positions Gomez 17 at GS-12, Hill 14, Jones 15; Ikeda at GS-9 is four grades below and excluded): must be offered Gomez's GS-12 position, the least reduction in rate. (d) If every offer is accepted, Brandt, Estrada and Dube are placed. Each displacement releases the incumbent: Ikeda (GS-9), Hill (GS-11) and Gomez (GS-12). Each is qualified only for the position held, so none has a qualifying assignment, and each is separated: Gomez, Hill and Ikeda. No one else is separated; Jones, Chen, Alvarez and Farouk remain.
Q12.uncertainty: The text does not say whether assignment rights extend to positions in the same competitive level (Farouk's GS-13 position is in the same level and held by a lower-standing employee, and literal 351.701(b) does not exclude it). I assumed the rights run to other competitive levels, which the table implies. The text also does not give an explicit chain of rights for displaced incumbents beyond 351.701(a)'s reference to 'displacing another employee under this part', so the separation of Gomez, Hill and Ikeda rests on their having no qualifying assignment, not on an express rule. Standing comparisons across different competitive levels are assumed to use the same scores.

Q13.answer: Items found in the main final rule, 91 FR 49178-49227, where a preamble statement differs from the amendatory instructions or regulatory text. (1) Tenure subgroup II and excluded appointments. Preamble, 91 FR 49196: subgroup II covers employees not serving an initial probationary period or 'a temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less'. Regulatory text, 351.502(a)(3), 91 FR 49220: subgroup II excludes 'a temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D of part 316' only (no term appointment). The excluded-employee text at 351.202(d)(2)(iii), 91 FR 49218, also says 'temporary appointment'. Another passage of the preamble, 91 FR 49191, describes the exclusion as 'temporary appointments of 1 year or less under subpart D' and matches the text. So the preamble's 'or term' wording is not borne out by the text. (2) Preamble description of the 351.503(c) window in Q12 terms is consistent with the text, so no item. I found no other clear preamble-to-text mismatch in the sections I checked (351.503(d), 351.504, 351.505, 351.507, 351.601(c), 351.608(c)-(f), 351.701(d) deletion, 351.805(b), the 180-day and 90-day competitive area rules, and the Implementation Considerations on effective dates). Those passages match the text.
Q13.uncertainty: This is not exhaustive. I checked a limited set of preamble statements against the text. The item in (1) is a discrepancy in wording and may be a drafting slip rather than a substantive difference, because the subpart D reference controls. The 60-day military spouse figure in the proposed rule's preamble is a proposed-rule point, excluded by the question.

Q14.answer: (i) Preamble-to-text mismatch in the appeals rule: the preamble says OPM 'does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs' and that, when agreements are renegotiated, the rule will limit bargaining for provisions creating a direct RIF appeal process inconsistent with part 351 (91 FR 49245, lines 1997-2004). The regulatory text, 351.901(c)(2) (91 FR 49263), says flatly that a RIF action taken under part 351 and any matter relating to its appeal 'may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration'. The text has no grandfathering for existing agreements and no renegotiation trigger. (ii) I did not verify an unacknowledged change from the proposed appeals rule to the final rule. The summary of changes (91 FR 49230-49232) acknowledges the items I checked, including the appealable-action language, the merits standard, exclusivity, e-filing, the tolling rule, the RIF notice content, the agency-record requirements, reply, disclosure limits, representatives and finality. I checked the proposed text of 351.909(a) (final decision after 30 days, proposed 2026-02576 p. 5877) and the proposed remedy text (p. 5876); both are acknowledged or unchanged. (iii) Inconsistency between the Board's rule and OPM's rule about which RIF appeals the Board still hears. The MSPB's regulatory text, 91 FR 51998 (new 1201.3(a)(5)), keeps only Foreign Service RIF appeals under 22 U.S.C. 4010a. Its DATES and preamble, 91 FR 51997, say MSPB 'will continue to adjudicate such ... RIF appeals' for agency actions taken before the effective date of OPM's rulemakings, and the preamble (91 FR 51997) keys this to RIF notices issued before that date. The MSPB DATES use 'agency actions taken before' while OPM's DATES (91 FR 49230) and the Dates of 2026-15665 (91 FR 49178) key the rule to issuance of a specific RIF notice on or after September 2. A RIF noticed August 31 with a separation after September 2 falls under the MSPB's 'actions taken' wording but not clearly under the Board's notice-based statement. The Board's text also contains no transitional provision matching its DATES statement.
Q14.uncertainty: The MSPB's own transitional wording is in its DATES and preamble, not in its regulatory text, so I cannot tell which controls. Item (i) may be read as limited to bargaining rights, not to the grievance bar; I flag it as an apparent tension. For item (ii) I did not complete a comparison, so I list none. The MSPB's codified 1201.3 list and the Foreign Service RIF scope are consistent with OPM's rule, since OPM's rule covers part 351 actions.
